transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Yeah, so... what finally pushed me to come in is, well, I keep getting up during meetings when I really know I should just stay put. Like during sprint planning for work—I'm a software developer, and we actually just switched our whole project management system over to Jira, which honestly has been a total nightmare because the migration lost half our active tickets, and my manager is just constantly stressing out about it. 

But anyway, during those long sprint calls, or even really important personal ones like my mortgage calls... my husband and I are looking into refinancing right now, though honestly I think we completely missed the boat on the good interest rates last year, it's just ridiculous. But yeah, during those calls, I just can't stay in my chair. I'll suddenly feel like I absolutely need to get a glass of water right that second, or I’ll just decide to go check something in the other room. I bought one of those big pitcher filters for the fridge and it takes forever to fill up, so I end up just standing in the kitchen... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right. Yeah, I just keep getting up and leaving my desk even when I know I'm supposed to be sitting there and paying attention.
Thinking back to when you were a kid in school, did you have similar trouble staying seated or focusing back then, or is this something that's really only become a problem more recently as an adult?

Oh, definitely back then too. I vividly remember my teachers in elementary school constantly having to move my desk. Like, Mrs. Miller in third grade... she actually put my desk right next to hers at the front of the room. She had this huge wooden desk, and I remember she always kept a jar of those little strawberry candies on it? The ones with the wrappers that look like actual strawberries? I haven't seen those in years, I wonder if they even still make them. 

But yeah, she had to keep me right there and was always reminding me to stay seated because I was just always popping up out of my chair. And I was always talking before I was called on, too. I'd just blurt out the answers. I actually understood the work perfectly fine, but I would just rush through everything so fast. I remember getting in trouble for my handwriting being a total disaster because I was just trying to get it done and move on. We were learning cursive that year, which, honestly, why did they make such a big deal out of cursive? They told us we'd use it every day as adults, and I literally never use it now. Everything is typing. I type like 90 words a minute now, probably because of all the coding and Slack messages. 

But wait, sorry, what did you ask? Oh, right, childhood. Yeah, it definitely happened when I was a kid too, not just recently.
Aside from the restlessness, have you been feeling persistently worried, on edge, or down and low in mood most days over the past few months?

No, honestly my mood is pretty good. I don't really feel down or worried about things. I mean, my husband is the one who gets really worried and on edge. Like with the refinancing stuff I mentioned, he tracks the interest rates every single morning. He has this massive Excel spreadsheet that he color-coded and everything. I actually had to help him set up a macro for it last weekend because he was updating the cells manually, which is just wild to me. 

I always tell the junior developers on my team—why do something manually when you can write a script for it in like ten minutes? They'll spend hours doing basic data entry and I'm just like, guys, Python exists for a reason! It's actually so satisfying when a script finally runs perfectly without throwing any syntax errors. I used to do a lot more hands-on coding before I got promoted, and I kind of miss it sometimes. The meetings are just endless now, which is why I bought that standing desk, actually. It's bamboo, really nice, but the delivery guy left it right at the bottom of the driveway... 

Wait, sorry, I'm doing it again. What did you ask me? Something about being sad? Yeah, no, I don't really get depressed or anxious. Just the not being able to sit still thing.

Do you also notice yourself frequently losing track of what you were doing, forgetting appointments or tasks, or having trouble sustaining attention on things even when you're not moving around, like when reading a report or filling out paperwork?

Yeah, for sure. Like, I can sit down to review a pull request at work, or read through those mortgage documents I mentioned, with totally good intentions to just focus and get it done. But after a few minutes, I’ll realize I’m just staring at the exact same section and my brain is off thinking about five completely unrelated things. 

Speaking of those mortgage documents, the bank sent them as this massive PDF, and it’s so annoying because Adobe Acrobat always tries to force you to sign up for their premium cloud subscription just to highlight text or add a signature. We use DocuSign at work, which is way smoother, though honestly their API has been giving us major headaches lately. One of our junior devs spent three entire days last week trying to figure out why the webhooks weren't firing, and it turned out to just be a firewall issue on our end. I always tell them to check the network logs first! Networking is honestly such a pain. I took a networking class for my bachelor's and the professor was this guy who wore a different patterned bowtie every single day. He had this whole collection... 

Wait, sorry, I completely lost the thread again. What did you ask? Oh, right, reading and paperwork. Yeah, I definitely lose track of what I'm reading and zone out even when I'm just sitting there.

latest_inference.note: Patient confirms both hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (childhood-onset restlessness, blurting answers, difficulty staying seated) and inattentive symptoms (losing track while reading, zoning out, distractibility), with no mood/anxiety symptoms reported. This combination supports combined presentation ADHD, ruling out F90.0 (predominantly hyperactive-impulsive) as the sole diagnosis.
